coverAlt: Illustrated cover for Advanced Combat System
title: Advanced Combat System
subtitle: Every hit should feel intentional.
imageAlt: Gameplay capture of the recallable axe combat prototype
summary: Directional melee, focus targeting, and a throwable, recallable axe. A combat playground built around timing, interaction, and responsive feedback.
overview: Advanced Combat System is a third-person C++ combat extension built on ALS Community. My work connects directional melee, defensive actions, weapon handling, target focus, and a throwable axe into a shared combat flow. The emphasis is on the relationship between input, animation, contact, and the response the player sees. The project extends an existing locomotion foundation with custom combat responsibilities. ALS Community supplies that foundation; the combat component, weapon interaction, and throw-and-recall behavior are the focus of this work.
contributions: C++ combat state, directional melee, animation-driven attack traces, and weapon switching.
Blocking, parry handling, directional dodge behavior, and target focus.
Throwable and recallable axe integration with character actions and weapon attachment.
Hit reactions, camera feedback, particles, and health presentation.
challenge: Connect a distinctive weapon mechanic to an existing locomotion and combat foundation without losing a clear relationship between player input and on-screen feedback.
approach: The combat component and axe implementation separate core combat behavior from the weapon-specific throw-and-recall interaction. Gameplay captures demonstrate the resulting interaction loop.
scope: Prototype built on ALS Community. The locomotion foundation is credited to that project; this showcase focuses on the custom combat and weapon work.

coverAlt: Illustrated cover for Modular Vehicle Builder
title: Modular Vehicle Builder
subtitle: Build it. Break it. Make it fly.
imageAlt: Gameplay capture from the modular vehicle construction sandbox
summary: Snap parts together, redistribute mass, and put a custom vehicle to the test. A build–drive–iterate sandbox with ground and flight modules.
overview: Modular Vehicle Builder is a Unity physics sandbox in which construction changes how a vehicle behaves. Players grab parts, align connection points, assemble a structure, and test it with wheels or propulsion modules. The same build can be revised after driving, making iteration part of the game. My contribution brings together part placement, rigidbody connections, runtime mass distribution, driving, and flight experiments. Rather than authoring a fixed vehicle for one scenario, the project explores how reusable physical components can form different player-made machines.
contributions: Attach points and physical joints for modular part connections.
Runtime center-of-mass updates and WheelCollider-based driving.
Propeller lift and aerodynamic surface logic for flight experiments.
A build, test, and iterate workflow supported by level progression code.
challenge: Let players assemble different shapes while keeping connections, mass distribution, and vehicle control responsive to the current construction.
approach: Dedicated attachment, mass, wheel, and propulsion components divide the physical responsibilities. This keeps each module focused while letting assembled parts influence the complete vehicle.
scope: An evolving construction and physics prototype. The earlier BadPigges experiments are linked below as related work. Current exploration includes flight modules and networked sessions.

title: TENLIVION EV
subtitle: A clearer path from station to session.
imageAlt: Actual Android demo screen showing the TENLIVION EV charging session
summary: A multilingual Flutter charging app with station discovery, connector selection, live session presentation, a demo wallet, and recovery-aware charging flows.
overview: TENLIVION EV is a Flutter customer application built around the complete charging journey: discover a station, choose the right connector, understand the price, start a session, follow its progress, and review the result. The Android demo combines these steps in a consistent mobile experience instead of treating them as disconnected forms. My work covers both the product interface and the application logic behind it. Alongside the map, charging screen, and wallet, the project includes explicit session states, recovery after interrupted operations, multilingual presentation, and a documented boundary for future backend integration.
contributions: Station map/list, search, filters, and favorites.
Station–EVSE–connector selection and visible kWh pricing.
Session start/stop flows, charging history, and a demo wallet.
Turkish, English, and Polish interfaces with light, dark, and system themes.
Separate data adapters and a documented backend contract for future integration.
challenge: Keep station availability, connector choice, charging progress, and payment-related states understandable across a connected mobile journey.
approach: Explicit screens and session states structure the experience, while data adapters separate the UI from the current mock data. The accompanying backend contract describes the integration boundary.
scope: Android prototype with mock stations, cards, and payments. Live payments, customer authentication, and OCPP integration are not connected. Screenshots are from the running Android demo.

coverAlt: Illustrated cover for Engine and Powertrain
title: Engine & Powertrain
subtitle: Make the machinery visible.
imageAlt: Capture of the engine and powertrain simulation showing mechanical components
summary: An interactive engine simulation connecting four-stroke cycles, sequential gearing, temperature, and mechanical feedback.
overview: Engine & Powertrain is an interactive Unity simulation connecting a four-stroke engine to a visible drivetrain. Throttle, fuel, engine temperature, gears, shaft rotation, differential output, and braking are represented by cooperating C# components. The goal is to make relationships between mechanical systems observable through interaction. My work focuses on the simulation logic and its presentation: an input changes engine behavior, mechanical outputs propagate through the drivetrain, and thermal or braking feedback explains what is happening. This is a gameplay and visualization project rather than a validated automotive engineering model.
contributions: Four-stroke engine phases, throttle/RPM response, and fuel consumption.
Thermal behavior, overheating cutoff, and cooling feedback.
Sequential gearbox with forward gears, neutral, reverse, and shift torque cuts.
Differential output splitting and brake heat visualization.
challenge: Connect engine, transmission, cooling, and braking behavior so that changes in one part are reflected elsewhere in the simulation.
approach: Engine, gearbox, cooling, differential, and brake scripts each own a specific mechanical responsibility. Visible shafts, temperature feedback, and effects make the interactions easier to inspect.
scope: Interactive simulation prototype focused on visualizing the relationship between mechanical systems and player-controlled inputs.

title: Multiplayer Parkour
subtitle: One obstacle course. Shared state.
imageAlt: Technical illustration of player input, server-owned moving platforms, and client synchronization
summary: A networked obstacle-course prototype exploring player ownership, synchronized moving platforms, knockback, and respawning.
overview: Multiplayer Parkour is a Unity Netcode for GameObjects project exploring how player-controlled movement interacts with a shared obstacle course. It includes local ownership checks, jumping, server-selected spawn points, synchronized moving platforms, collision knockback, and respawning. My focus is the boundary between what a player controls and what the shared world owns. Movement needs to respond to the local player, while obstacles and lifecycle events need a consistent interpretation across the session.
contributions: Owner-controlled player movement and jumping.
Server-assigned spawn positions and multiplayer respawning.
Server-updated moving platforms with client synchronization.
Collision-driven knockback and a host/client entry interface.
challenge: Separate player-owned input from shared world behavior so every participant can interact with the same moving obstacles.
approach: Player ownership gates movement input, while platform state is updated on the server. RPC-based messages coordinate platform updates, knockback, and respawn events.
scope: A networked gameplay study using Unity Netcode for GameObjects. The technical diagram above illustrates the implemented ownership and synchronization model.

title: Factory Check
subtitle: Keep operational context connected.
imageAlt: Factory floorplan asset used in the Factory Check project, not an application screenshot
summary: A Flutter/Firebase operations app connecting incident ownership, machine downtime, immutable shift handovers, team calendars, reports, and read acknowledgements.
overview: Factory Check is a Flutter and Firebase application for coordinating factory incidents across monitoring, operators, maintenance, and support teams. It follows an issue from the initial report through ownership, intervention, production recovery, and resolution, while preserving the notes and shift context that explain what happened. My work connects the mobile workflow to operational data: machine status, incident history, responsibility transfers, downtime intervals, shift planning, end-of-shift reports, and read acknowledgements. The result is a field-test application that treats continuity between people and shifts as part of the core workflow.
contributions: Incident lifecycle from open and assigned to intervention and resolved.
Role-aware team filters, notes, photos, and event history.
Shift handover, responsibility transfer, and employee/shift planning.
Machine downtime intervals, period reports, and read acknowledgements.
Turkish, English, and Polish support with Firebase-backed data and authentication.
challenge: Preserve the history and ownership of an operational issue as people, shifts, and incident states change.
approach: Incident workflows are combined with Firestore records, authentication, and storage for supporting media. Handover and reporting screens keep responsibility and operational context visible.
scope: Field-test build. Notification functions exist in source but deployment is not established. The image is the project's factory layout asset, not a screen capture of the application.

title: Dark Descent
subtitle: Combat and skills in a dark fantasy world.
summary: A dark fantasy action project built with a multidisciplinary team. My contribution focused on core gameplay, skill-system implementation, and player interactions.
overview: Dark Descent is a collaborative action game with a dark fantasy setting. A Templar journeys through limbo, fighting demons and lost souls while trying to recover his faith. The published project describes fast combat and a magic system built around combining Holy, Fire, and Order. My contribution focused on gameplay programming, the skill system, and player interactions. This showcase concentrates on that programming role within the team's wider game, art, and narrative production.
contributions: Core gameplay programming.
Skill-system implementation and player interactions.
Collaboration with the wider team to connect mechanics and narrative intent.
challenge: Support exploration and tension through gameplay systems that fit the team's intended experience.
approach: My work concentrated on the player's interaction loop and skill behavior, developed in collaboration with the other disciplines on the team.
scope: A multidisciplinary team project. My focus was gameplay programming; the full game and its artwork are collaborative work.

coverAlt: Illustrated cover for The Last Branch
title: The Last Branch
subtitle: Parkour and gameplay in an Unreal Engine adventure.
imageAlt: The Last Branch game artwork from the original portfolio
summary: An Unreal Engine adventure made with a multidisciplinary team. My work focused on parkour and player-facing gameplay mechanics.
overview: The Last Branch is a collaborative Unreal Engine adventure about exploring an abandoned temple as a child of the Godtree. The published game places the player among lost spirits and an infestation of Rot, with a journey toward restoring life beyond the temple. My contribution was parkour and gameplay mechanics. I worked on the behavior through which the player navigates and interacts with the game, as part of a wider production involving programming, design, art, animation, audio, and quality assurance.
contributions: Parkour and traversal gameplay programming.
Player-facing gameplay mechanics within the Unreal Engine project.
Integration of my mechanics with the team’s shared game experience.
challenge: Integrate parkour and gameplay mechanics into a shared Unreal Engine adventure.
approach: Implement player-facing behavior within the multidisciplinary team’s game.
scope: Collaborative Unreal Engine adventure. My contribution focused on parkour and gameplay mechanics.

title: Vampire
subtitle: A compact combat and progression loop.
imageAlt: Technical illustration of the Vampire prototype's combat, enemy escalation, and XP upgrade loop
summary: Top-down combat combining mouse-directed attacks, orbiting weapons, enemy escalation, and an XP-driven upgrade loop.
overview: Vampire is a Unity 2D arena-combat project connecting player movement, aimed attacks, an orbiting weapon, ammunition, enemy spawning, health, and experience-based progression. It includes the menu and recovery states around the combat, so the interaction forms a repeatable run rather than stopping at a weapon demonstration. My work brings the systems together around player state. Experience changes the encounter mix and unlocks an upgrade choice; damage changes the health display and can lead to game over; restarting returns the player to the combat loop.
contributions: Movement, mouse-directed weapon rotation, and an orbiting weapon.
Health, experience, levels, and upgrade choices.
Escalating melee, archer, and boss spawning.
Ammunition UI, pause/resume, retry, and game-over states.
challenge: Make combat, enemy escalation, and progression cooperate within a small, playable prototype.
approach: Player and spawner scripts connect level state to enemy variety and upgrade choices. Menu and retry controls close the loop around the core combat experiment.
scope: A compact gameplay prototype exploring combat and progression. The technical diagram above illustrates the implemented gameplay loop.

title: Tower Defence
subtitle: Distinct tower behaviors. Connected combat systems.
imageAlt: Gameplay screenshot of the tower defence game-jam project
summary: A Unity team game with arrow, bomb, and escalating-damage towers, spline-following enemies, respawn behavior, and gold-based unit spawning.
overview: This Unity team project connects tower combat, enemy movement, and an economy-driven spawning loop. Different tower behaviors create distinct pressures along the path: targeted arrows, bomb projectiles, and a sustained inferno attack that becomes stronger while it stays on a target. My portfolio contribution focuses on tower behavior, attack and defense mechanics, and enemy encounters. The source shows a more specific set of systems than a generic tower-defence description: shared health and respawning, path-aware targeting, spline movement, collision pushback, and gold/cooldown constraints on spawning.
contributions: Tower types with projectile and sustained-damage attack behavior.
Attack and defense gameplay integrated with shared health and respawn systems.
Enemy encounter and spawning work within the team's gameplay loop.
challenge: Connect tower behavior and enemy waves into a playable loop under game-jam time constraints.
approach: The work centered on the systems that determine how towers engage enemies and how waves progress, then integrating those systems with the team's wider game.
scope: Team game-jam project. My work focused on towers, combat behavior, and enemy waves, integrated with the team's visuals and wider game.

title: Apo’nun Köyü
subtitle: Farming, livelihood, and village politics.
summary: A first-person village-life game connecting farming, trade, a configurable economy, quests, dialogue, vehicles, building, and persistent world state.
overview: Apo’nun Köyü is an independently developed first-person village-life game set in rural Anatolia. Farming, inventory, trading, vehicles, quests, dialogue, and cinematic storytelling form a connected experience shaped by economic pressure and local political satire. My work covers the game's interconnected systems and the tools used to create its content: reusable quest steps, crop definitions, dialogue authoring, world-state tracking, vehicle configuration, and save/load coordination. The project includes a substantial playable systems foundation alongside active content and integration work.
contributions: Design and development of the connected farming, inventory, trading, and economy systems.
Modular quests, dialogue, cinematic sequences, and custom Unity authoring tools.
Vehicle interactions, construction, daily progression, and world-state integration.
Save/load coordination for player, quest, inventory, crop, building, and vehicle data.
challenge: Carry an exploration concept across several disciplines and bring the parts together into one coherent prototype.
approach: The project combines player-control work, environment iteration, and gameplay scripting in a single Unity production.
scope: Independent Unity prototype, developed across concept, gameplay, and environment integration.

coverAlt: Illustrated cover for Snake in Unreal
title: Snake in Unreal
subtitle: Small game. Explicit fundamentals.
imageAlt: Original image from the Unreal Engine Snake project repository
summary: An Unreal Engine C++ Snake project with grid movement, dynamic growth, text-authored levels, BFS pathfinding, local player/AI modes, and level progression.
overview: Snake in Unreal is a C++ gameplay project that develops the classic collection-and-growth loop into a broader systems exercise. Beyond movement and tail segments, the source includes text-authored levels, an AI controller using breadth-first search, local human/AI modes, score presentation, and progression between levels. My work explores Unreal's division between pawn, controller, world actor, game mode, and widgets. The familiar rules make the engineering easy to inspect: where movement is decided, how a board is generated, how an opponent finds food, and how a completed level changes the game state.
contributions: C++ player control, snake growth, food collection, collision, and scoring.
Text-authored level generation with instanced floor and wall meshes.
Breadth-first-search AI using walkable tiles and tail occupancy.
Local player/AI mode logic, level progression, menus, and input-state transitions.
challenge: Express a familiar game loop through Unreal's actor model and C++ gameplay code.
approach: The project concentrates on a small set of readable mechanics and their lifecycle: spawn, move, collect, grow, collide, and restart.
scope: A C++ gameplay programming study built in Unreal Engine, with a deliberately compact scope.
